primer.chn_p_world.title: All Under Heaven
primer.chn_p_world.text: You were born in the Middle Kingdom, the centre of the world under the rule of the Son of Heaven. Over these centuries three dynasties will rise and fall: the Song with its scholar-officials, the Mongol Yuan and the Chinese Ming. The emperor governs through thousands of officials who passed the examinations, and every county has its yamen, a government office with a drum at the gate. More than a hundred million people live here, more than in all of Europe. Yet danger always comes from the steppe to the north.
primer.chn_p_world_nsong.title: Northern Song
primer.chn_p_world_nsong.text: You were born under the Northern Song. In 960 the general Zhao Kuangyin put on the emperor's yellow robe and founded a dynasty with its capital at Kaifeng. Scholars, not generals, run the country: power goes to those who pass the examinations. The Khitan Liao press from the north, and under a treaty of 1005 they receive 100,000 taels of silver and 200,000 bolts of silk every year to keep the peace. At court, men argue bitterly over the reforms of the minister Wang Anshi.
primer.chn_p_world_ssong.title: A Divided Land
primer.chn_p_world_ssong.text: You were born in a divided land. In 1127 the Jurchens took Kaifeng and carried off two emperors. Prince Zhao Gou fled south, and from 1138 the Southern Song court has sat at Hangzhou, with the border along the Huai River. General Yue Fei, who longed to win back the north, was executed in 1142, and people still sing of him. The south grows rich on rice and sea trade, but from the 1230s it is the Mongols, not the Jurchens, who hold the north.
primer.chn_p_world_jin.title: Under the Jin
primer.chn_p_world_jin.text: You were born in Kaifeng, which is no longer the Song capital. In 1127 the city fell to the Jurchens, a forest people from the northeast who founded the Jin, the 'Golden' empire. First a puppet state called Qi ruled here, then Kaifeng became the Southern Capital of the Jin. Peasants till the same fields, and many Chinese officials serve the new masters and sit examinations on the same books. But half the palaces stand empty, and many families have kin who fled south.
primer.chn_p_world_yuan.title: The Mongol Yuan
primer.chn_p_world_yuan.text: You were born under the Mongols. Khubilai, grandson of Genghis Khan, named his realm Yuan in 1271, took Hangzhou in 1276, and in 1279 the last Song fleet perished off Yamen. The capital is now Dadu, today's Beijing. People are sorted into four ranks: Mongols, semu or 'various peoples' from the west, northern Han, and lowest of all the southerners, though historians debate how strictly this worked. The examinations are suspended until 1315, and paper money called chao is everywhere.
primer.chn_p_world_ming_early.title: The Early Ming
primer.chn_p_world_ming_early.text: You were born under the young Ming, the 'Bright' dynasty. Its founder, Zhu Yuanzhang, a former beggar monk and leader of the Red Turban rebels, drove out the Mongols in 1368. He reigned as the Hongwu emperor and had tens of thousands of suspects executed. His son, the Yongle emperor, moved the capital from Nanjing to Beijing, and from 1405 the fleets of the eunuch Zheng He sailed seven times to India and Africa. In 1449 the Oirats captured the emperor himself.
primer.chn_p_world_ming_late.title: The Late Ming
primer.chn_p_world_ming_late.text: You were born in the late Ming. The empire is vast and rich: the Great Wall is being rebuilt in brick, and silver flows in through Manila and Japanese ports, from the 1570s even from the Americas. Taxes are converted into silver under the 'Single Whip' reform. Wokou pirates raid the coast, from 1592 Ming armies fight the Japanese in Korea, and the Manchus grow strong in the northeast. The Wanli emperor refuses to meet his officials for decades. In 1644 the rebel Li Zicheng will take Beijing.
primer.chn_p_society.title: The Four Occupations
primer.chn_p_society.text: Confucians divide the people into four occupations: at the top the shi, scholars; then the nong, farmers who feed the land; below them the gong, artisans; and last the shang, merchants, who 'produce nothing'. In practice a rich merchant lives far better than a poor scholar. There is almost no hereditary nobility: high office comes through the examinations, which nearly any man may sit. At the very bottom are the 'mean people' — servants, actors, in some places boatmen — and for them the examination hall is closed.
primer.chn_p_society_slave.title: Nubi
primer.chn_p_society_slave.text: You were born to a family of nubi, servants without rights. People fall into bondage through debt, through famine when parents sell their children, or as punishment for a relative's crime. Under the Song many serve on contracts for a fixed term; under the Mongols servitude more often becomes hereditary; Ming law forbids commoners to keep nubi at all, leaving it to officials and nobles. A master can give you away as part of a dowry, marry you off or set you free. The law punishes killing a servant, but beating one is allowed.
primer.chn_p_society_peasant.title: Tenant Farmers
primer.chn_p_society_peasant.text: You were born to a family of tenant farmers, dianhu. The land belongs to a landlord, and the rent is paid in grain, up to half the harvest. Anyone with a plot of his own pays tax twice a year, in summer and autumn, and everyone owes labour: mending dykes, hauling grain. The village is bound by mutual responsibility — baojia under the Song, lijia groups of 110 households under the Ming. But since the eleventh century a fast-ripening rice from Champa has spread across the south, and in good years it yields two harvests.
primer.chn_p_society_noble.title: An Official's House
primer.chn_p_society_noble.text: You were born in the house of a high official. Your father's rank shows from afar: a purple or crimson robe, a belt with plaques of jade or gold, and under the Ming an embroidered square on the chest — a crane for the highest civil ranks. People bow before him, and he travels in a sedan chair. Sons of great officials can receive posts on their father's merit, without examinations, but true honour belongs only to those who pass. A single fall from favour can cost the family everything.
primer.chn_p_birth.title: The First Month
primer.chn_p_birth.text: The moment you were born you were already one year old: in China age is counted from birth, and another year is added every New Year. On the third day the baby is bathed in herbal water, and the mother spends a month 'sitting' at home — no washing, no going out in the wind, chicken broth with ginger. After a month there is a celebration with sweets for the guests. On the first birthday a brush, a book, coins and a needle are laid before the child, and whatever it grabs foretells its future.
primer.chn_p_childhood.title: Filial Piety
primer.chn_p_childhood.text: The first virtue of a child is xiao, filial piety: obey your parents, feed them in old age, honour the ancestors. Children hear the tales of the 'Twenty-Four Paragons of Filial Piety' — like the boy who let mosquitoes bite him on summer nights so they would spare his parents. Sons of well-off families begin learning the Three Character Classic and the Thousand Character Classic at six or seven, reciting them aloud until they know every line. Peasant children herd water buffalo, carry water and mind the little ones.
primer.chn_p_childhood_girl.title: Bound Feet
primer.chn_p_childhood_girl.text: In many families a girl's feet begin to be bound when she is five to seven: a long strip of cloth folds the toes under the sole so the foot stays small. It takes years and is very painful, and it changes how a woman walks for the rest of her life. A tiny foot is called a 'golden lotus' and seen as a mark of beauty and good upbringing that helps a girl marry well. The custom began among the elite under the Song and spread more widely by the Ming, yet many poor families and whole regions never practised it.
primer.chn_p_home.title: House and Courtyard
primer.chn_p_home.text: A house faces south behind a wall, its rooms opening onto an inner courtyard. In the north people sleep on a kang, a wide brick platform warmed by smoke from the stove; in the south the walls are wooden and the floors raised against the damp. Under the Song the Chinese finally moved from floor mats to chairs and tall tables. Windows are covered with paper, a charcoal brazier glows in the corner, and in Kaifeng people even burn coal. Above the stove hangs a paper image of the Kitchen God.
primer.chn_p_food.title: Rice and Tea
primer.chn_p_food.text: The saying goes that seven things are needed every day: firewood, rice, oil, salt, soybean paste, vinegar and tea. The south eats rice; the north eats wheat noodles, flatbreads and steamed buns, and the poor eat millet and beans. Meat usually means pork, and mostly on feast days. Tofu and pickles appear at every meal, everyone eats with chopsticks, and everyone drinks tea, from the emperor to the porter. Cities have restaurants serving dishes from every region, and in the late Ming sweet potatoes and maize arrive from overseas.
primer.chn_p_clothes.title: Robes and Caps
primer.chn_p_clothes.text: Ordinary people wear a short jacket and trousers of hemp or ramie, and from the fourteenth century more and more often of cotton, which people learned to weave well in Songjiang — thanks, it is said, to a weaver named Huang Daopo. The rich wear long silk robes with wide sleeves. Men never cut their hair; they gather it in a knot under a cap or a net. Yellow is for the emperor alone, and the law spells out who may wear which fabrics and patterns.
primer.chn_p_faith.title: The Three Teachings
primer.chn_p_faith.text: People in China speak of the 'Three Teachings': Confucianism teaches duty and order, Buddhism compassion and release from suffering, Daoism harmony with the Way and long life. Most people don't choose just one: at a funeral both Buddhist monks and Daoist priests are invited. Every home keeps ancestor tablets, and every town has a temple to the City God, guardian of its walls. Under the Song the scholar Zhu Xi reinterpreted Confucius, and his commentaries will become required reading for the examinations.
primer.chn_p_faith_folk.title: Ancestors and Spirits
primer.chn_p_faith_folk.text: Your family honours its ancestors: every morning incense is lit before their tablets with tea and rice, and at the Qingming festival the whole family goes to sweep the graves. Paper money is burned for the dead so they have something to live on in the other world. The Kitchen God watches the household all year, and on the twenty-third day of the last month he flies up to Heaven to report on the family — so his lips are smeared with sticky sweets. Sailors in the south pray to the goddess Mazu.
primer.chn_p_faith_buddhist.title: The Buddha's Path
primer.chn_p_faith_buddhist.text: Your family honours the Buddha. Many lay people tell their beads and repeat 'Amituofo', the name of Amitabha Buddha, hoping to be reborn in the Pure Land of the West. Most beloved of all is merciful Guanyin, to whom people pray for children and rescue. In mountain monasteries monks practise Chan, the path of seated meditation. Becoming a monk requires a government certificate, and the Song treasury even sold them. On feast days people bring oil and money to the temples, and on fast days they eat no meat.
primer.chn_p_faith_islam.title: China's Muslims
primer.chn_p_faith_islam.text: Your family follows Islam, like the descendants of Arab and Persian merchants who settled in the ports and of newcomers from Central Asia. Quanzhou has a stone mosque with a tall gateway, Guangzhou a minaret that doubles as a lighthouse. Under the Mongols Muslims serve as tax collectors, governors and astronomers; under the Ming their descendants speak Chinese, bear Chinese names and are called Hui. The famous admiral Zheng He was a Muslim too. Your family does not eat pork.
primer.chn_p_faith_jewish.title: The Jews of Kaifeng
primer.chn_p_faith_jewish.text: Your family belongs to the small Jewish community of Kaifeng, whose ancestors most likely came from Persia along the trade routes. In 1163 the community built a synagogue, where Torah scrolls are kept and the Sabbath is observed. Neighbours call them the 'teaching that removes the sinew', because Jews do not eat the sciatic nerve of animals. The community lives among the Chinese, speaks Chinese, and many of its sons sit the examinations. There are only a few hundred such families — you belong to a rare people.
primer.chn_p_faith_christian.title: China's Christians
primer.chn_p_faith_christian.text: Your family is Christian, a rare faith here. Under the Mongols Christians are called yelikewen; most follow the Church of the East and come from steppe peoples and Central Asia. From 1307 Dadu has a Catholic archbishop, John of Montecorvino, and Quanzhou has Franciscan bishops; gravestones there are carved with a cross rising from a lotus. After the fall of the Yuan these communities all but vanished, and not until 1601 will the Jesuit Matteo Ricci arrive in Beijing.
primer.chn_p_work.title: Strings of Cash
primer.chn_p_work.text: Money in China means bronze coins with a square hole, threaded on a cord: a string, a guan, holds a thousand. They are heavy to carry, so in Sichuan people invented paper money, and from 1024 the state prints it. Craftsmen are organised in guilds called hang, and each street has its trade. Salt, tea and wine are state monopolies. Grain taxes travel north along the Grand Canal, and later, under the Ming, accounts shift to silver, which is cut and weighed.
primer.chn_p_place.title: Your Land
primer.chn_p_place.text: China is immense: in the north the dusty plains of the Yellow River, wheat and cold winters; in the south rice paddies, canals and bamboo; in the west, mountains. The Yellow River is called 'China's Sorrow': more than once it has changed course and washed whole counties away. People from different regions can barely understand each other's speech, yet they all write the same characters. The land, people say, rests on three things: dykes, canals and grain in the state granaries.
primer.chn_p_place_kaifeng.title: City on the Bian
primer.chn_p_place_kaifeng.text: Kaifeng stands on the Bian Canal, where barges bring rice up from the south. Under the Northern Song perhaps a million people lived here, and the night markets traded until dawn. Above the city rises the Iron Pagoda, named for its rust-brown glazed tiles. It is said that this very life — bridges, boats, eating houses, camels at the gates — is what Zhang Zeduan painted on the scroll 'Along the River During the Qingming Festival'. After 1127 the capital emptied, and the nearby Yellow River flooded the city more than once.
primer.chn_p_place_hangzhou.title: By the West Lake
primer.chn_p_place_hangzhou.text: Hangzhou lies on the West Lake at the southern end of the Grand Canal. A causeway built by the poet Su Shi crosses the lake, the Leifeng Pagoda rises over the water, and boats carry singing girls across it. When the Southern Song court was here the city was called Lin'an, and by some estimates more than a million people lived in it. Silk is woven here, and tea grows on the hills. Fire is feared more than any enemy: the wooden quarters burn often.
primer.chn_p_place_quanzhou.title: The Port of Zayton
primer.chn_p_place_quanzhou.text: Arabs and Persians call Quanzhou Zayton, and in the thirteenth and fourteenth centuries it is one of the greatest ports in the world. A maritime trade office has worked here since 1087. Four-masted junks crowd the harbour, warehouses hold pepper, frankincense and ivory, and silk and porcelain leave for distant shores. Two stone pagodas rise over the Kaiyuan Temple, a mosque stands nearby, and by the sea people pray to the goddess Mazu. Under the Ming sea trade is banned, and the port declines.
primer.chn_p_place_chengdu.title: City of Hibiscus
primer.chn_p_place_chengdu.text: Chengdu lies in the Sichuan Basin and is called Rongcheng, 'City of Hibiscus', after the flowers once planted on its walls. Its fields are watered by the Dujiangyan canals, built more than a thousand years ago, and harvests here are steadier than anywhere else. The city is famous for its Shu brocade, its tea and its Sichuan pepper, which makes the tongue go numb. It was here that merchants first invented paper money. From the 1230s to the 1270s wars with the Mongols devastated Sichuan; how many died is still debated.
primer.chn_p_place_beijing.title: The Great Capital
primer.chn_p_place_beijing.text: Beijing began as Dadu, Khubilai's 'Great Capital' with straight streets; it is said the Mongol nobles pitched yurts even there. Under the Ming the Yongle emperor built the Forbidden City here, finished by 1420, and beside it the Temple of Heaven, where the emperor prays for good harvests. In spring a yellow wind blows dust in from the desert; winters are bitterly cold. Camel caravans carry coal through the streets, and the Great Wall is a day or two's journey north.
primer.chn_p_law.title: Justice at the Yamen
primer.chn_p_law.text: Justice is done by the county magistrate at his yamen: a drum hangs at the gate, and striking it lodges a complaint. The magistrate is investigator, prosecutor and judge at once, and the law allows suspects to be tortured. There are five punishments: the light stick, the heavy stick, penal labour, exile and death. A whole family can be punished for one member's crime. The honest judge Bao Zheng, who governed Kaifeng in the 1050s, became a folk hero; it is said no one could ever bribe him.
primer.chn_p_health.title: Doctors and Remedies
primer.chn_p_health.text: Doctors feel the pulse at three points on the wrist, insert needles and burn mugwort on the skin. Under the Song the state opened pharmacies selling cheap medicines, and in 1027 bronze figures were cast with holes at the needling points to train acupuncturists. The worst diseases are smallpox, fevers in the humid south and great epidemics, especially in the 1330s to 1350s. In 1578 Li Shizhen will complete the Bencao Gangmu, describing nearly 1,900 remedies. The poor go to a folk healer or to the temple.
primer.chn_p_women.title: The Inner Quarters
primer.chn_p_women.text: The saying goes: men outside, women inside. A girl is married at fifteen to eighteen through a matchmaker and carried in a red sedan chair to her husband's family, where the mother-in-law rules. Under the Song her dowry counts as her own property, and a widow may take it with her. Neo-Confucians insist that widows stay faithful, and under the Ming the most steadfast are honoured with stone arches. Yet there were poets like Li Qingzhao, and wives who ran the affairs of whole households.
primer.chn_p_women_peasant.title: He Ploughs, She Weaves
primer.chn_p_women_peasant.text: Farming families say: the man ploughs, the woman weaves. Your mother, most likely from a village much like this one, raises silkworms and spins hemp or cotton, and part of the family's tax is paid in her cloth. In spring the women go out to transplant rice; the rest of the time they cook, fetch water and look after children and parents-in-law. In poor families girls' feet are bound less often or less tightly: you cannot work in a paddy on 'golden lotuses'.
primer.chn_p_leisure.title: Festivals and Fairs
primer.chn_p_leisure.text: The year opens with the Spring Festival: firecrackers bang, and fresh images of door gods go up on the gates. Fifteen days later comes the Lantern Festival, in spring Qingming, in summer the dragon-boat races, in autumn the Moon Festival with round cakes. Kaifeng and Hangzhou have pleasure quarters called wazi, full of storytellers, puppeteers, acrobats and theatre. People play xiangqi chess, fly kites, and even the court kicks a cuju ball. Under the Yuan, musical drama flourishes.
primer.chn_p_knowledge.title: The Examinations
primer.chn_p_knowledge.text: The road upward runs through the examinations: county, prefectural, metropolitan, and finally the palace examination before the emperor himself. Those who pass the highest level are called jinshi; in some years only a few hundred in the whole country. Candidates spend days shut in cramped cells writing essays on the classics. Books are printed from carved wooden blocks, and around 1040 a craftsman named Bi Sheng invented movable type made of clay. In 1408 the Yongle Encyclopedia will be compiled — more than 11,000 volumes.
primer.chn_p_war.title: The Wall and Gunpowder
primer.chn_p_war.text: The great enemy is the steppe: Khitans, Tanguts, Jurchens, Mongols, later the Oirats and the Manchus. The Song army numbers over a million, and soldiers are tattooed on the face or hands so they cannot desert. Gunpowder was invented here: fire lances, bombs, rocket arrows. Under the Ming soldiers come from hereditary 'military households', and the Great Wall is rebuilt in brick. In the 1550s and 1560s General Qi Jiguang crushes the wokou pirates on the coast.
